articles.title: The DMZ from Hue: What Each Stop Actually Shows You
articles.excerpt: The DMZ tour from Hue is a long day with a dozen possible stops, and the standard circuit picks them for the driver's convenience. Here is what each one shows, so you can pick for yours.
articles.content:
The Demilitarised Zone was the strip of land either side of the Ben Hai river, on the seventeenth parallel, that divided Vietnam from 1954 to 1975. Tours from Hue cover it in a long day, and most of them run the same circuit. The stops are far apart and not equal, and the standard order is built around driving distance rather than meaning. If you know what each one shows, you can shape the day, or decide that a private car and three stops beats a minibus and seven.

The Ben Hai river and the Hien Luong bridge

The Ben Hai river at the Hien Luong bridge is the line itself: the seventeenth parallel, the border between North and South Vietnam from the Geneva settlement of 1954 until reunification. The bridge is a restored steel span painted in two colours, one for each side, with a flag tower on the northern bank and a monument of a mother and child facing north. A museum on the bank tells the story from the Vietnamese side.

What it shows you is the arbitrariness: a modest river in flat country, and the fact that for twenty years families lived on opposite banks unable to cross. Allow half an hour. It is the stop with the most symbolic weight and the least to walk around, and it is usually the first because it is on the highway north.

Doc Mieu and the coastal strip

Doc Mieu was an American firebase on the southern bank, part of the electronic barrier that was meant to seal the border. Little remains and most tours mention it from the road. It shows you the geography of the war's northern front: the sea on one side, the hills on the other, and a river in between.

The Vinh Moc tunnels

Vinh Moc, on the coast north of the river, is a tunnel complex where a fishing village moved underground to survive years of bombardment, with living chambers, a meeting hall, a well and exits onto the beach. It differs from the better-known tunnels near Ho Chi Minh City in that it was dug for civilians to live in rather than for fighters to move through, and the passages are reported to be close to their original size rather than widened for visitors.

Vinh Moc is the stop the day is built around and the one that justifies it. You go underground on a guided route with lighting; it is confined, humid and dark, and anyone uneasy in enclosed spaces should know that before the entrance. Allow an hour and a half with the small museum. If you have a private car and only want one stop beyond the bridge, this is it.

Truong Son national cemetery

Truong Son is the largest of Vietnam's war cemeteries, inland from Highway 1, holding the graves of soldiers who died along the Ho Chi Minh trail, laid out by home province under pine trees. It is a working national shrine rather than a tourist site, and Vietnamese visitors come to burn incense and leave offerings. Many of the graves carry no name.

It shows you the war's cost on the Vietnamese side at a scale no museum manages, and it is the stop Americans most often say changed how they saw the day. It is not on every circuit because it is off the direct route to Khe Sanh. Ask for it.

Conduct

Shoulders and knees covered, hats off at the central memorial, and photographs of the grounds rather than of people praying. The same applies at the smaller cemeteries the road passes.

Khe Sanh combat base

Khe Sanh is the former US Marine base in the hills near the Laos border, besieged for months in early 1968 in one of the war's most reported battles, and later abandoned. What remains is a reconstructed bunker or two, some aircraft and vehicles on a plateau, and a museum whose displays tell the siege from the Vietnamese perspective. The red earth and the surrounding hills are the real exhibit.

It shows you where the American war was fought on the ground, and for a veteran's family it is often the reason for the day. For anyone else it is a long drive west for a quiet field. It is the stop that makes the tour ten hours rather than seven, and the one to drop if you want a shorter day.

The road to it

Route 9 west from the highway passes the Rockpile, a steep outcrop that served as an American observation post, and the Dakrong bridge, a reconstruction over a river that was part of the trail network. Both are roadside stops of a few minutes, and the minibus tours include them because they are on the way.

What most tours leave out

Quang Tri town, on Highway 1 south of the river, was flattened in the eighty-one-day battle of 1972 and the shell of a church and the citadel walls still stand. It is closer to Hue than anything else on the list and almost never on the circuit, because the circuit is sold as the DMZ and Quang Tri is technically south of it.

For a sense of what the ground war did to a town, it says more than Khe Sanh.

Unexploded ordnance

The province is still being cleared, and the sites you visit are safe to walk; the risk is in fields and construction sites, not at monuments. The State Department's assessment is that landmine risk is low in urban and populated areas, including tourist destinations. Stay on paths and touch nothing metal in the ground, and that is the whole of the precaution.

Shaping your day

Minibus tours give you the full circuit at the lowest price and the longest day, with the stops fixed. A private car costs more per person for one or two and about the same for four, and it lets you choose: bridge, Vinh Moc and Truong Son in a seven-hour day, or everything including Khe Sanh in a long one. Book a DMZ tour from Hue, or arrange a car and name the stops yourself.

The guide matters more than the vehicle. A good one has family stories; a bad one reads the plaques.

articles.title: Ha Giang Loop: Ride It Yourself, Ride Pillion, or Go by Car
articles.excerpt: The loop is the best road in Vietnam and the one place the licence question stops being theoretical. Here is what each of the three ways of doing it actually gives you.
articles.content:
The Ha Giang loop is a several-day circuit of mountain road in Vietnam's far north, up against the Chinese border, through the Dong Van karst plateau and over the Ma Pi Leng pass. It has become the thing travellers in their twenties go to Vietnam for, and the photographs are not exaggerating. The question is not whether to go. It is how to do the road, because the three ways of doing it are not three prices for the same thing.

What the loop is

The Ha Giang loop runs north from Ha Giang city through Quan Ba and Yen Minh to Dong Van, then along the Ma Pi Leng pass above the Nho Que river to Meo Vac, and back by a different road. Most people take three or four days.

The stretch between Dong Van and Meo Vac has no public transport worth the name, so everyone does it on a motorbike or in a hired vehicle, and that is where the decision lives.

Ha Giang city is most of a day from Hanoi by road, and the loop starts and ends in Ha Giang city, where the rental shops, the tour companies and the hostels cluster. The road is paved for the most part but narrow, with blind bends, livestock, trucks and long drops, and it is mountain weather: fog in winter, heavy rain in summer.

Why it is not Sapa

Sapa is a town with treks around it. Ha Giang is a road with villages along it. You do not base yourself anywhere; you move every day, and the point is the moving. That is also why the mode question matters more here than anywhere else in Vietnam.

Riding it yourself

Riding the Ha Giang loop on your own rented motorbike is the version sold hardest, and for an American it has a legal problem that does not go away. A US driver's licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, and the State Department says plainly that driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail. Renting without one is illegal, whatever the shop says.

The shop will rent to you anyway. That is the part that misleads people, and it does not change the position. Under Vietnam's traffic law, driving without the licence the law requires is itself a listed prohibited act, and police do stop riders on the loop. The usual outcome of being stopped is a fine, but the more serious exposure is the one you do not feel until something goes wrong: after an accident while riding unlicensed, your travel insurance may not pay your medical bills. On a road with drops like these, and with the nearest serious hospital a long way off, that is the number that matters.

What you read about the IDP

You will find a confident claim that a particular edition of the International Driving Permit works in Vietnam. The US government's statement to its own citizens is that neither your licence nor your IDP works, and that is what we go by. If you have ridden for years at home and want to ride here, the honest version is that you would be doing it unlicensed and uninsured, and deciding that the road is worth it.

Riding pillion with a local rider

Riding pillion on the Ha Giang loop means a licensed local rider drives, you sit behind with a small bag, and a van carries the rest. It is the version most tour companies in Ha Giang city now sell, often called an Easy Rider trip, and it is the only one that gives you the road on two wheels without the licence problem. The rider knows the bends, the weather and the places to stop.

You still wear a helmet, and so does the rider: every rider and every passenger on a motorbike must wear a helmet with the chin strap fastened, pillion passengers included. A good operator issues them; a bad one hands you a plastic shell. Check.

What you give up

Control of the pace, mostly. You stop where the group stops, and on a busy week the groups all stop at the same viewpoints at the same time. Ask whether the trip is a convoy of twenty bikes or a few, and whether the riders speak enough English to tell you what you are looking at. Both vary widely between operators, and the price difference between them is small compared with the difference in the days.

Going by car

A car with a driver covers the Ha Giang loop on the same roads in the same number of days, and it is the right choice for more people than the hostel culture around the loop suggests. Anyone travelling with a parent, anyone who does not want four days of cold or rain on a bike, anyone carrying camera gear, and anyone who simply does not want to be a passenger on a motorbike for hours at a time will see the same landscape through a windscreen.

What you lose is specific: the wind, the smell of the villages, the ability to stop anywhere on a whim, and the particular feeling of the Ma Pi Leng pass from a saddle rather than a seat. People who have done both describe the car version as seeing the loop and the bike version as being in it. That is a real difference, and it is also a smaller one than the loop's reputation implies.

When the car wins outright

In the winter fog, in heavy summer rain, and for anyone whose trip would be wrecked by a minor spill. A fall at walking pace on gravel is the common Ha Giang accident, and in a car it does not happen.

How to choose

Choose pillion if you want the road itself and are fit enough to sit on a motorbike for several hours a day. Choose the car if you are travelling with anyone who would not enjoy that, or if your dates fall in fog or monsoon.

Riding yourself is the choice we cannot recommend to an American, because it means riding unlicensed and probably uninsured on the most consequential road in the country; if you do it anyway, do it knowing that, not believing the shop.

Booking

Book a Ha Giang loop tour from Hanoi or in Ha Giang city; the Hanoi bookings include the overnight bus or van north. Whatever you book, confirm the helmet, the group size and whether there is a support vehicle, because those three things are the trip.

What this decision sits inside

Notice what settled the Ha Giang question: not the scenery, which is the same in all three versions, but the licence, the insurance and the weather. The same three things decide the Hai Van Pass between Hue and Da Nang, the Dalat road down to the coast, and whether you rent a scooter for a week on Phu Quoc. Most people answer each of those separately and end up inconsistent, insured on one road and not on the next.

The connected version, which road is worth which mode for your dates and your party, is worked out in the complete Vietnam decision manual.

articles.title: How Many Days Hue Deserves
articles.excerpt: Three well-known guidebooks give Hue three different answers, from skipping it to two full days. The right number depends on what you came to Vietnam for, and here is the rule.
articles.content:
Hue is the city every Vietnam itinerary trips over. It was the imperial capital under the Nguyen dynasty, it has the citadel and the royal tombs, and it sits on the way between Hanoi and Hoi An. Yet one major guidebook's two-week plan skips it entirely, another gives it a single night, a third gives it two full days. None of them says why. Here is the answer, keyed to what you actually want from the trip.

The short answer

Hue deserves two nights, giving one full day, for a first-time visitor who cares about history; three nights if the DMZ matters to you; and one night as a stop on the way through if your trip is about beaches, food and Hoi An. Zero is defensible only on a seven-day trip that is choosing between the centre and the north or south, and even then the Hai Van train ride argues for passing through.

Why the books disagree

Because they are answering different travellers. The plan that skips Hue is written for a coast-and-cities trip. The plan that gives it two days is written for the citadel and the tombs. Neither is wrong; they just never told you whose trip they were planning.

What one full day covers

One full day in Hue covers the Imperial City in the morning, when it is cooler and quieter, and two of the royal tombs in the afternoon, usually Tu Duc and Khai Dinh, with Thien Mu pagoda on the river on the way. That is the Hue most visitors want, and it fits between arriving the previous evening and leaving the next morning. It is brisk but it is not rushed.

The tombs are spread through the countryside south and west of the city, each emperor having built his own, and they are deliberately unalike: Minh Mang formal and symmetrical, Tu Duc rambling and overgrown, Khai Dinh a dark concrete hybrid of Vietnamese and European styles. Two of the three is the right number. All three is a long afternoon in which the third starts to look like the second.

What the single night loses

Arriving at midday and leaving the next morning gives you an afternoon, which means the citadel or the tombs but not both done properly. Many itineraries do exactly this on the way between Hanoi and Hoi An. It works, and it leaves people saying Hue was fine, which is the sound of a place seen at half strength.

What the second full day adds

A second full day in Hue is for the DMZ or for the food, and rarely both. The Demilitarised Zone and the Vinh Moc tunnels are a long day north of the city, often ten to twelve hours door to door, and they are the reason some visitors give Hue an extra night.

Without that day you can still see the third tomb, the covered market, the garden houses in the suburbs and an evening on the river, at an easier pace.

Hue's food is the other argument for staying. It is the centre's own cuisine: bun bo Hue, the tiny steamed rice cakes served in sets, the baby-clam rice, and a vegetarian tradition from the city's pagodas. A day with no sights lets you eat it at the right hours, which the sightseeing day does not.

Who should take the second day

Americans with a family connection to the war, for whom the DMZ day is the point of the central coast. Anyone who has already done Hoi An's tailors and beaches on a previous trip. Anyone whose idea of a good day is a market and a long lunch rather than a monument.

Where the days come from

Hue's nights come out of Hoi An's in almost every itinerary, because the two are a few hours apart and the central coast gets a fixed allocation. On a two-week trip the common split is two nights in Hue and three in Hoi An. On ten days it is one and three, or two and two.

On a week, the centre gets three nights total and the honest choice is Hoi An plus a Hue day trip from Da Nang, or Hue plus the train and a Hoi An night.

The train between Hue and Da Nang over the Hai Van pass is the one transfer in Vietnam worth doing for its own sake, and it is why passing through Hue on the way to Hoi An costs almost nothing in time. Flying over it costs the view.

The weather caveat

Hue's rain comes in the autumn and early winter and it is heavy, with flooding in the bad years. The citadel in a downpour is an endurance event. If your dates fall then, one night is enough and the second day belongs to Hoi An, which gets the same weather but has more to do indoors.

A rule you can apply

History first: two nights, and a third if the DMZ is on your list. Food and beaches first: one night on the way through, with the train. Seven days or fewer: Hue is a day trip from Da Nang or a pass-through, not a base. Where to stay in Hue matters less than in Hoi An; the south bank near the river is the sensible default for a night or two.

What this question is really part of

Notice what decided Hue's days: not Hue, but the length of your trip and the nights already committed to Hoi An, Hanoi and the south. Every base on the central coast is paid for out of the same pool, and the books that disagree about Hue are really disagreeing about the pool.

Deciding the whole allocation at once, nights per base by trip length and by whether you came for history, beach or food, is worked out in the complete Vietnam decision manual.

articles.title: Phong Nha Caves: Which Tour Fits Your Trip and Your Budget
articles.excerpt: Phong Nha has caves you can walk into in an afternoon and one that takes a week and a serious bank balance. Here is how the options sort themselves by time, fitness and money.
articles.content:
Phong Nha-Ke Bang is the cave region of central Vietnam, a UNESCO-listed national park of limestone mountains riddled with some of the largest cave passages on earth. It sits north of Hue, with the town of Dong Hoi as its gateway, and it has gone from a backpacker secret to a fixture on first-time itineraries. The difficulty is that "visiting Phong Nha" covers everything from an hour on a boat to a six-day expedition, and the names on the tour boards do not tell you which is which.

The caves, sorted by effort

Phong Nha's caves fall into three bands: the show caves you can see in a day with no fitness at all, the adventure caves that take a day or two with some walking, swimming or kayaking, and Son Doong, which is a multi-day expedition in its own category. Most visitors want the first band and are sold the second; a few want the third and should book it a long way ahead.

Show caves: the day with no effort

Phong Nha cave itself is reached by boat along the river from the village, and the boat carries you into the cave mouth and along the underground river. Paradise Cave is a dry cave with wooden walkways and lighting, entered on foot down a staircase, with a long formation-filled passage you walk along at your own pace. Either is an afternoon; the two together are a full day with lunch. Neither needs anything but shoes you can walk in.

Adventure caves: a day or two, some sweat

Dark Cave is the entry-level adventure, sold as a package of a zipline across the river, a swim into the cave mouth, a wade through a mud chamber and a kayak back. It is noisy, popular and fun, and it is not a serious caving trip. The step up is a one- or two-day trek with a licensed operator into caves such as Hang En, where you sleep on a sandy beach inside the cave, or the Tu Lan system, where the route involves swimming through flooded passages. These need a reasonable level of fitness and a tolerance for being wet for hours.

Son Doong: the one that costs a trip

Hang Son Doong, the largest known cave passage in the world, is visited only on one operator's multi-day expedition. Oxalis Adventure sells it as a six-day, five-night expedition priced at VND 80,000,000, about USD 3,000, per person, graded challenging, with about a day and a half of jungle trekking before you reach the cave mouth.

The number of places each year is small and the season is limited, so this is booked many months ahead, not decided in Dong Hoi.

For most first-time visitors to Vietnam, Son Doong is not the question. It is a trip you plan a holiday around, not a stop you add to one. If it is the point of your journey, it decides your dates, your fitness training and a week of the itinerary before anything else is booked.

Who it suits

Fit, patient people who want a once-in-a-lifetime expedition and have the budget for it. Anyone who hesitates on any of those three should look at Hang En instead, which is run by the same kind of operator, gives you a night camping inside an enormous cave, and costs a fraction of the money and the time.

Where Phong Nha fits in an itinerary

Phong Nha costs a first-time itinerary about four days: a day to get there from Hue or Hanoi, two days in the park, and a day to leave. The gateway town is Dong Hoi, with a railway station on the north-south line and a small airport, and the park village is a further transfer inland.

The cheap day trips sold out of Hue exist, but they spend most of the day on the road and reach only the show caves, rushed.

So the real decision is what those four days displace. On a two-week trip they usually come out of the central coast or the Mekong. On three weeks they fit without strain. Phong Nha also sits naturally between Hue and the north, so a north-to-south route that stops there on the way down costs less in backtracking than a detour out of Hue and back.

The two-day version that works

Arrive in the afternoon, do Paradise Cave or the Phong Nha river cave the next morning and Dark Cave or a countryside bicycle ride in the afternoon, then an adventure cave on the second full day if you want one, and leave on the third morning. That gives you both bands of cave without an expedition.

Booking and season

The show caves can be done independently or through any guesthouse. The adventure caves and Son Doong are sold only through licensed operators, and you should book Phong Nha cave tours before you arrive in the busy months, because the overnight trips have fixed group sizes. Check the operator's licence for the specific cave; the national park restricts which caves can be entered and with whom.

Season matters more here than in most of Vietnam. The park's rivers rise sharply in the central coast's wet months in the autumn, and the adventure caves close when they flood. The dry, hot months are the reliable window; the river cave is at its best when the water is clear.

What to bring

Shoes that can get wet and still grip, a dry bag for a phone, and clothes you do not mind leaving muddy. The operators supply helmets and headlamps for the adventure caves. The show caves need nothing you do not already have.

articles.title: Two Days from Hanoi: Boat on Ha Long or Rowboat in Ninh Binh
articles.excerpt: Most short trips have two days to spend outside Hanoi, and the same limestone scenery is on offer by sea or by river. The choice turns on weather, travel time and what kind of day you want.
articles.content:
A first trip to northern Vietnam usually has two days to give the landscape outside Hanoi, and the two obvious ways to spend them show you the same thing from different sides. Ha Long Bay is the limestone karst at sea, seen from a boat you sleep on. Ninh Binh is the same karst inland, seen from a rowboat on a river between rice fields. Guidebooks list both and leave the choice to you. Here is how to make it.

The short answer

Ninh Binh is the better use of two days for most first-time visitors in winter, for anyone prone to seasickness, and for anyone who wants to move at their own pace. Ha Long Bay is the better use for anyone whose dates fall in the calm months and who wants the night on the water, which is the thing the day trips cannot give.

If you have two days and are unsure, the deciding factor is the weather forecast for your dates, not the photographs.

Why not both

Because both in two days means a day trip to each, and the Ha Long day trip is the weakest version of Ha Long there is. Two days gives you one place done properly. Three or four lets you do an overnight on the bay and a day in Ninh Binh, which is the combination the longer itineraries use.

What each costs you in travel

Ha Long Bay and Ninh Binh are both reachable from Hanoi in a morning. Hanoi to Ha Long city by road is about 2.5 hours since the expressway and the Bach Dang bridge opened in 2018; guidebooks that still say four hours were printed before the road. Ninh Binh is about two hours south, by road or by train. The difference in transfer time is small; the difference is in what happens when you arrive.

At Ha Long you board a boat on a fixed schedule and the boat decides your day. At Ninh Binh you are on land with a bicycle or a driver, and you decide your day. A two-day Ha Long trip is therefore one night aboard with a short second morning. A two-day Ninh Binh trip is a full day and a half of sights, because nothing is waiting for you to embark.

The weather problem is Ha Long's alone

Ha Long Bay cruises are cancelled by the port authority, not by the operator, whenever a storm or dangerous weather is forecast: the provincial waterways port authority stops issuing departure permits to every tourist vessel, day boats and overnight cruises alike. Operators refund or reschedule, but a two-day window has no room to reschedule into. Ninh Binh's rowboats run in rain; a wet day there is a worse day, not a lost one.

The winter months in the north bring fog and drizzle that sell well in photographs and poorly in person: a grey bay with the islands half visible, and the real risk of a suspension. Late spring, and again from early autumn into November, give the best odds of clear air and calm water; summer is the busiest season on the bay and the one that brings storm cancellations. If your two days fall in a winter forecast of low cloud, Ninh Binh is the safer bet by a distance.

If the cruise is cancelled

Have Ninh Binh as the fallback in your head before you leave Hanoi. A cancelled cruise on the morning of departure can be turned into a Ninh Binh day trip from the same hotel, which is why the two places are substitutes and not just alternatives.

What kind of day you get

A Ha Long overnight is a cruise: cabins, meals aboard, a kayak session, a cave, a swim, the evening light on the water and the morning before the day boats arrive. It is passive in the pleasant sense, and it is the one experience of the bay that the crowds cannot spoil, because the overnight boats anchor away from the day-trip circuit.

A Ninh Binh day is active. The Trang An boat route passes through water caves and past temples for two to three hours; Tam Coc is shorter, prettier in the golden rice weeks, and more commercial. Between boats there is the climb to the Hang Mua viewpoint, Bai Dinh pagoda, and the countryside by bicycle. People who like to be doing something every hour prefer it, and people who want to sit still with a drink prefer the boat.

Children, older travellers and seasickness

Both work for families. The bay in calm weather is gentle; a rolling bay is miserable, and the forecast settles that. Ninh Binh's climbs are optional and its boats are flat-water. Anyone who is unsteady on their feet will find a cruise boat's stairs harder than a rowboat's bench.

How to decide

Check the forecast for your two dates. Calm and clear: book the Ha Long overnight, because the night on the bay is the better of the two experiences when the weather lets it be. Cloud, wind or a storm warning: go to Ninh Binh and spend the second night there rather than back in Hanoi. Seasick, short of time or travelling with someone who tires: Ninh Binh regardless.

Book a Ninh Binh day tour or a Ha Long Bay overnight cruise once that call is made, and hold the other as the fallback.

What this choice is really part of

Notice that the deciding factor was the month, not the place. The same month decides whether Sapa's terraces are green or brown, whether Hue is flooded, and whether the beaches at the other end of the country are in season. A trip that chooses Ha Long for its dates and then arrives at the coast in its wet weeks has answered one question correctly and the others not at all.

The month-by-region table that resolves them together, with a verdict for each pair, is the spine of the complete Vietnam decision manual.
